name: Sant tradition (nirguṇa bhakti of North India)
alt_names: Sant Mat (older generic sense: 'the doctrine of the Sants')

tradition.text: Kabīr is placed by his panth in 1398–1518 (a life of 120 years); the Sants count Nāmdev and the other bhagats before Kabīr as their forerunners

scholarly.text: Sant poetry from the 15th c. (Kabīr c. 1440–1518 on many accounts; Ch. Vaudeville argued 1398–1448), with the Maharashtrian Nāmdev (c. 1270–1350) as forerunner; panths organized 16th–18th c.

transmissions_received.what: yogic vocabulary: sahaj, śūnya, the unstruck sound (anāhad), the tenth door, the sky-circle (gagan-maṇḍal), the address 'avadhū', upside-down speech (ulaṭbāṃsī)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared vocabulary; Kabīr's songs address the avadhū (Nāth yogī); see brw:natha-to-sant

transmissions_received.what: the name of Rām; the tradition that Rāmānanda initiated Kabīr, Ravidās, Pīpā, Sen and Dhannā
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account (Anantadās's Paracaīs; Nābhādās's Bhaktamāl); disputed by the Kabīr Panth and doubted by scholars on chronological grounds; see dsp:kabir-guru-ramananda

transmissions_received.what: Nāmdev's Hindi padas; Nāmdev venerated as a Sant forerunner (named by Ravidās)
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit mention: Ravidās's pad 'aisī lāl tujh binu kaunu karai' names Nāmdev, Kabīr, Trilocan, Sadhnā and Sain

transmissions_given.what: the Sant poets as authorities; Kabīr, Paltū, Tulsī Sāhib and others cited as masters of the inner sound current

distinctive_positions: The ultimate is nirguṇa (beyond attributes) and yet is loved: it is called Rām, Hari, Sāhib, Alakh, Nirañjan, Satnām — Rām not as the son of Daśaratha but as the one who pervades all.
The Name (nām) and the Word (śabd), revealed by the true guru (satguru), are the means; outward repetition on beads without the mind is rejected.
The true guru is praised as highly as God, sometimes higher ('guru and Govind both stand before me — whose feet shall I touch?').
The divine is within the body (ghaṭ); temple and mosque, idols, pilgrimage, ritual bathing, fasting, sectarian garb, the Veda and the Qur'ān, Hindu and Turk forms are all rejected as outward.
Caste has no standing before God; many Sants were of low or 'untouchable' birth (weaver, leatherworker, barber, cotton-carder) and spoke of it openly.
Liberation is sought now, in this body: 'dying while living' (jīvan-mṛtak), the natural state (sahaj), in the company of sants (satsang), mostly as householders at honest work.
Teaching is sung in the vernacular: sākhī couplets, pad/śabd songs and ramainī verses, gathered in anthologies arranged by topic (aṅg).
summary: The Sants are the poet-saints of North India, from Kabīr, Ravidās and Dādū onward, who taught love of a formless God (nirguṇa bhakti) through the Name and the true guru, located the divine within the body, and rejected caste, idols, pilgrimage, scripture-learning and the rival formalisms of Hindus and Muslims. Their songs were gathered into anthologies and their followers formed panths (Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth, Ravidāsī, Nirañjanī, Rāmsnehī, Caraṇdāsī, Satnāmī, Garībdāsī); the nineteenth-century Sant Mat (Radhasoami) is their recent heir.
notes: Family 'vedic' is used here for the Hindu side of the ontology, as for other bhakti lineages; the Sants themselves reject the authority of both Veda and Kitāb (Qur'ān). The Sikh Gurus are counted among the Sants by many scholars and the Ādi Granth (1604) preserves Kabīr, Ravidās, Nāmdev and other bhagats; Sikh scripture is outside this ontology's scope and is noted as context only. Exchanges with Sufis are recorded as context only (Sufism is outside scope). The Maharashtrian Vārkarī saints are the 'southern Sants' (owned by U26).

name: Kabīr Panth

tradition.text: founded by Kabīr's disciples after his departure at Maghar (1518 in the panth's reckoning)

scholarly.text: organized as a panth with monastic seats by the 17th c.; the Dharamdāsī line's written corpus (Kabīr Sāgar, Anurāg Sāgar) is dated by scholars to the 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: Kabīr is the incarnation of the Sat Puruṣ (the True Being) who descends in every age to free souls (haṃs) from Kāl (in the Dharamdāsī literature: as Sat Sukṛt, Munīndra, Karuṇāmay and Kabīr in the four ages).
A cosmogony (Anurāg Sāgar) in which Kāl Nirañjan, a fallen son of the Sat Puruṣ, creates and rules the three worlds and binds souls; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are his sons.
Initiation (dīkṣā) with a kaṇṭhī necklace; in the Dharamdāsī line also the pān-parvānā and the caukā rite.
Two main branches: the celibate Kabīr Chaurā line in Varanasi, whose scripture is the Bījak, and the Dharamdāsī line of 42 generations of householder ācāryas in Chhattisgarh.
Vegetarianism, abstention from intoxicants, and rejection of caste distinctions within the panth are enjoined.
summary: The Kabīr Panth is the organized following of Kabīr, with monastic and householder members, sādhus and mahants, initiation and ritual. It venerates Kabīr as the incarnate True Being, which stands in some tension with Kabīr's own rejection of ritual and of worshipping persons; its Dharamdāsī branch developed an elaborate cosmogony of Kāl Nirañjan and the Sat Puruṣ.
notes: Scholarly studies (e.g. D. N. Lorenzen, F. E. Keay) are used only for dating labels.

name: Kabīr Chaurā Maṭh (Mūl Gādī), Varanasi

tradition.text: founded by Surat Gopāl, Kabīr's disciple (panth account)

distinctive_positions: Celibate succession of mahants at the site of Kabīr's teaching in Varanasi.
The Bījak is the scripture; the Dharamdāsī cosmogony is less central here.
summary: The monastic seat of the Kabīr Panth in Varanasi, at the place where Kabīr is said to have lived and taught; its line traces itself to Surat Gopāl.

name: Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth (Chhattisgarhī śākhā)

tradition.text: Kabīr promised Dharamdās a line of forty-two generations (vaṃś) of ācāryas

scholarly.text: the line's texts and seats are dated by scholars to the 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: A hereditary line of householder ācāryas beginning with Dharamdās's son Cūṛāmaṇi (Muktāmaṇi) Nām.
The Anurāg Sāgar's cosmogony of Kāl Nirañjan and the Sat Puruṣ, and the caukā ritual with the pān-parvānā (betel-leaf 'passport') for souls.
Kabīr as the Sat Puruṣ incarnate.
summary: The largest branch of the Kabīr Panth, centred in Chhattisgarh among many lower-caste and tribal followers, led by a hereditary line of ācāryas from Dharamdās.

name: Dādū Panth

tradition.text: Dādū Dayāl, 1544–1603; his fifty-two disciples founded fifty-two seats (thāmbā)

scholarly.text: late 16th c. onward; the Vāṇī compiled by the early 17th c.; the anthologies (Pañcvāṇī, Sarvāṅgī) from the 17th c.

transmissions_received.what: Kabīr's songs, which the Dādūpanthī anthologies preserve alongside Dādū's
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit: the Pañcvāṇī collects Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās and Hardās with Dādū

distinctive_positions: Remembrance of the nirguṇa Rām, the one God of Hindu and Turk, without idols or temples.
Impartiality (nipakh) and the middle way (madh): neither Hindu nor Turk, neither indulgence nor harsh austerity.
The guru met 'in the unseen' (gaib) and devotion to the guru; the Vāṇī itself is honoured in the panth's seats.
Five divisions in the later panth: Khālsā (the Naraina seat), Virakt (wandering renunciants), Uttarādhī, Khākī and the armed Nāgā.
Anthologies arranged by aṅg (topic), which preserved much of the Rajasthani Kabīr.
summary: The panth founded by Dādū Dayāl (1544–1603) in Rajasthan, with its chief seat at Naraina. It preserved Dādū's Vāṇī and, in its anthologies, the western recension of Kabīr and other Sants; its scholars (Rajjab, Sundardās) gave the Sant teaching systematic and learned form.
notes: Division names and the 'fifty-two disciples' are from the panth's tradition as commonly reported; moderate confidence.

name: Ravidāsī (Ravidassia) tradition
alt_names: Ravidassia Dharam (2010 designation of Dera Sachkhand Ballan)
regions: Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh

tradition.text: Guru Ravidās is dated by his followers from 1377 (birth celebrated on Māgh Pūrṇimā); tradition gives him a very long life

scholarly.text: Ravidās flourished in the 15th–early 16th c.; the organized Ravidāsī community and its deras are 19th–20th c.; Ād Dharm 1925; Ravidassia Dharam declared 2010

distinctive_positions: Ravidās, a leatherworker (Camār) of Banaras, is the guru; his hymns are the scripture.
Begampura, the 'city without sorrow', where there is no tax, no fear, no second or third class, is the goal and the ideal.
Rejection of caste and untouchability; dignity of the Camār community.
The relation of self and God is like gold and bracelet, water and wave: 'between you and me, me and you, what difference?'
Since 2010 the Dera Sachkhand Ballan line has a separate scripture (Amritbāṇī) and symbol (Har), distinct from the Sikh Ādi Granth.
summary: The community and religious tradition of the followers of Guru Ravidās (Raidās), predominantly of the Camār (leatherworker) caste. It venerates Ravidās's hymns (forty preserved in the Ādi Granth, more in Rajasthani manuscripts), his vision of Begampura and his rejection of caste; in the 20th c. it organized around deras in Punjab and declared a separate Ravidassia Dharam in 2010.
notes: The modern organized forms (deras, Ād Dharm 1925, Ravidassia Dharam 2010) are post-1800 and flagged recent; Ravidās himself is pre-modern.

name: Nirañjanī sampradāya

scholarly.text: 16th–17th c. (Haridās Nirañjanī's dates uncertain)

distinctive_positions: Worship of Nirañjan, the stainless formless one, joining Nāth yogic language with Sant devotion.
Praised by Rajasthani anthologists alongside the Dādūpanthīs.
summary: A Rajasthani Sant sampradāya founded by Haridās Nirañjanī that names the ultimate Nirañjan and stands between the Nāth yogīs and the Sants.

name: Rāmsnehī sampradāya

scholarly.text: 18th c.; Rāmcaraṇ (1720–1798) at Shāhpurā

distinctive_positions: Remembrance of the nirguṇa Rām as the sole practice; no images.
Several independent seats (Shāhpurā, Rain, Sinhthal, Kheṛāpā), each with its own founder.
Renunciant sādhus in distinctive (pink/ochre) dress and householder followers.
summary: An eighteenth-century Rajasthani Sant sampradāya of 'lovers of Rām', with seats at Shāhpurā (Rāmcaraṇ), Rain (Dariyāv Sāhib), Sinhthal and Kheṛāpā.

name: Caraṇdāsī sampradāya
alt_names: Śuka-sampradāya (because Caraṇdās's guru is said to be Śukadeva)

tradition.text: Caraṇdās received initiation from Śukadeva (the Bhāgavata's Śuka) in person

scholarly.text: 18th c.; Caraṇdās 1703–1782

distinctive_positions: A synthesis of Sant nirguṇa devotion with Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa devotion and aṣṭāṅga yoga.
The guru is exalted above Hari (Sahajobāī).
Notable women teachers: Sahajobāī and Dayābāī.
summary: The Delhi sampradāya of Caraṇdās (1703–1782), which joined nirguṇa Sant teaching with Kṛṣṇa devotion and yoga, and is remembered for its women poet-saints Sahajobāī and Dayābāī.

name: Satnāmī movements

scholarly.text: three movements sharing the name: Narnaul (17th c.; rising of 1672), Jagjīvandās (1670s–1761), Ghāsīdās (early 19th c.)

distinctive_positions: The 'true name' (sat nām) of the formless God as the centre of practice.
Rejection of images and (in Chhattisgarh) of caste hierarchy; the Chhattisgarh Satnāmīs are largely of Camār origin.
Vegetarianism and abstention from intoxicants (Ghāsīdās's rules).
summary: Several distinct Sant movements named after the 'true name': the Satnāmīs of Narnaul (Bīrbhān, 17th c.), the Satnāmī sampradāya of Jagjīvandās in Awadh (18th c.), and the Satnāmī panth of Ghāsīdās in Chhattisgarh (19th c., flagged recent).
notes: One id covers three historically separate movements that share the name; they may need splitting after sourcing.

name: Garībdāsī panth

scholarly.text: 18th c.; Garībdās 1717–1778

distinctive_positions: Kabīr is the supreme God, who met Garībdās in person as a child.
Garībdās's Bāṇī (his 'Granth Sāhib') is the scripture.
summary: The panth of Garībdās of Chhuḍānī (1717–1778), a Jat householder saint who held Kabīr to be the supreme God and left a large collection of Sant verse.

name: Sant Mat (Radhasoami and its successor lines)
alt_names: Sant Mat ('the teaching of the Sants', modern specific sense)

tradition.text: public satsang opened by Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji Maharaj) at Agra on Basant Pañcamī 1861

scholarly.text: founded 1861 at Agra; branches from 1878 onward (Agra lines, Beas 1891, Dayalbagh 1915, Ruhani Satsang 1951)

transmissions_received.what: the older Sants (Kabīr, Nānak as context, Tulsī Sāhib, Paltū, Dariyā) read as teachers of the inner sound current
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation in Sār Bachan and in the Beas and Ruhani Satsang literature

distinctive_positions: Surat-śabd yoga: the soul (surat) is withdrawn to the eye centre and rises by attaching itself to the audible life stream (śabd, dhun) through inner regions to its source.
The necessity of a living Sant Satguru, who initiates (nām-dān) and guides the soul inwardly.
Creation in grand divisions — piṇḍ (physical), aṇḍ, brahmāṇḍ (ruled by Kāl, the negative power), above which are the purely spiritual regions of Dayāl up to Anāmī / Radhasoami Dhām.
Practice as simran (repetition of the names given at initiation), dhyān (contemplation of the Master's form) and bhajan (listening to the sound).
Vows at initiation: lacto-vegetarian diet, no alcohol or drugs, a moral life, daily meditation (two and a half hours in the Beas line).
summary: The modern Sant Mat, begun in 1861 at Agra by Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji Maharaj) as Radhasoami, teaches the ascent of the soul on the inner sound current under a living master. It divided into the Agra lines (Soamibagh, Peepal Mandi, Dayalbagh), Radha Soami Satsang Beas, Kirpal Singh's Ruhani Satsang and its successors, Maharshi Mehi's Santmat of Bihar and others.
notes: Post-1800: flagged recent. Western derivatives (e.g. Eckankar, MSIA) are outside scope and not recorded.

name: Radhasoami Satsang, Agra lines (Soamibagh, Peepal Mandi / Huzuri Bhawan, Dayalbagh)

scholarly.text: from 1878 (Soamiji's death); Dayalbagh colony founded 1915

distinctive_positions: 'Radhasoami' is the true name of the supreme being, revealed by Soamiji.
Soamiji and his successors as the incarnation of the Supreme (Sant Satguru).
Dayalbagh: a planned community joining spiritual practice with work, industry and education.
summary: The Agra branches of Radhasoami after Soamiji: Soamibagh (Soamiji's family and followers), Peepal Mandi / Huzuri Bhawan (Rai Salig Ram's line) and Dayalbagh (from 1915 under Anand Swarup).

name: Radha Soami Satsang Beas

scholarly.text: from 1891 (Jaimal Singh settled at Beas); successors Sawan Singh 1903–1948, Jagat Singh 1948–1951, Charan Singh 1951–1990, Gurinder Singh Dhillon from 1990

distinctive_positions: The five names given at initiation (held confidential) and the five sounds of the inner regions.
Strict separation from ritual; the teaching presented as the universal core of all religions.
Seva (voluntary service) and the Dera as a working community.
summary: The largest Sant Mat organization, founded at Beas in the Punjab by Baba Jaimal Singh (a disciple of Soamiji), which spread the teaching worldwide under Sawan Singh and Charan Singh.
notes: A successor-designate (Jasdeep Singh Gill) was announced in 2024 (moderate confidence).

name: Ruhani Satsang and its successor missions
alt_names: Sawan Kirpal Ruhani Mission / Science of Spirituality

scholarly.text: founded 1951 by Kirpal Singh after Sawan Singh's death; successor missions from 1974

distinctive_positions: The same surat-śabd yoga, with emphasis on the first-hand inner experience given at initiation and on self-introspection (the daily diary).
Unity of man; the teaching presented as the science of the soul.
summary: The line of Kirpal Singh (1894–1974), a disciple of Sawan Singh, who founded Ruhani Satsang in Delhi in 1951; after him the line divided among Darshan Singh (then Rajinder Singh), Thakar Singh, Ajaib Singh and others.

name: Santmat Satsang of Maharshi Mehi (Bihar)

scholarly.text: 20th c.; Maharshi Mehi 1885–1986

distinctive_positions: Santmat as the common teaching of the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and the Sants, compiled in the Satsang Yog.
Graded practice: mental repetition (mānas jap), mental contemplation of form (mānas dhyān), point-focus (dṛṣṭi yoga) and then the inner sound (nādānusandhān).
summary: A Bihar Santmat lineage founded by Maharshi Mehi Paramhans, independent of the Radhasoami organizations, teaching the inner light and sound in a Vedāntic-Sant synthesis.

name: Bāul

scholarly.text: the word bāula (a madman of God) appears in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 19, Advaita's riddle); Bāuls as a distinct community are documented from the 18th–19th c.; Lalon Fakir d. 1890

transmissions_received.what: the sahaja doctrine, the body as the place of the divine couple, rasa and rati, the practice of the couple, secret language
body-yoga vocabulary: reversal (ulṭā), the tenth door, the lotuses and currents
the Vraja līlā, Caitanya and Nityānanda as figures of the songs, nāma-kīrtana
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit mention in the songs (e.g. Lalon's 'tin pāgale holo melā nadey ese')

distinctive_positions: The Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ), the Unknown Bird (achin pākhi), the Uncatchable Man (adhar mānuṣ) dwells in this body; he is to be sought within, not in temple, mosque or scripture.
Body-theology (deha-tattva): 'what is in the vessel (the body) is in the universe' (je āche bhāṇḍe tā āche brahmāṇḍe).
What is present and verifiable in the body (bartamān) is trusted over inference, hearsay and scripture (anumān).
Caste and religious labels are rejected: 'everyone asks what caste Lalon is; I have never seen the form of caste'.
The guru (murśid) is the living human through whom the Man is found; worship of the human (mānuṣ bhajan).
The song (gān) is teaching, practice and code: sung with the ektārā and dotārā at ākhṛās and melās.
A secret practice of the couple and of the bodily substances, reversing the downward flow (ulṭā / ujān sādhanā) — recorded here only in summary (restricted).
summary: The Bāuls are wandering and householder singer-practitioners of Bengal, both Hindu (Vaiṣṇava-Sahajiyā-derived) and Muslim (Fakir), who seek the Man of the Heart within the human body under a living guru, reject caste, scripture and sectarian worship, and teach through songs; Lalon Fakir (d. 1890) is their most celebrated master.
notes: Family 'shared' because the tradition draws on Vaiṣṇava, Nāth and (on a scholarly hypothesis) Buddhist Sahajiyā streams and includes Muslim Fakirs; the Sufi side is recorded as context only. Most Bāul teaching is oral and much of it is deliberately secret; many teachers are post-1800 and flagged recent.

name: Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā

tradition.text: the tradition claims Jayadeva, Vidyāpati, Caṇḍīdās, Caitanya, Rūpa, Sanātana and Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja as Sahajiyā masters

scholarly.text: Sahajiyā texts are post-Caitanya, mostly 17th–18th c.; continuity with the Buddhist Sahajiyā of the Caryāgīti is a scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Rūpa Gosvāmī's rasa theory, the parakīyā ideal, Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body, the Caitanya-caritāmṛta's kāma/prema distinction
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit citation and re-reading (e.g. Vivartavilāsa on the Caitanya-caritāmṛta)

transmissions_received.what: sahaja as the innate goal, the body as microcosm, the union of the two principles, songs in coded language
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis (S. B. Dasgupta, Obscure Religious Cults) supported by shared vocabulary with the Caryāgīti

distinctive_positions: Every man and woman has two natures: the outward form (rūpa) and the divine nature (svarūpa) — Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman.
By superimposition (āropa) of svarūpa on rūpa, human love (kāma) is transformed into divine love (prema), 'as gold is purified from ore'.
The parakīyā (love outside marriage) of the gopīs is taken as the model for human practice between partners — recorded in summary only (restricted).
The sahaja mānuṣa, the innate Man, dwells in the body; the goal is the sahaja state beyond the play of the two.
A graded path: pravarta (beginner, with name and mantra), sādhaka (practitioner, with bhāva), siddha (perfected, with prema).
Caitanya and the Gosvāmīs are read as secret Sahajiyās; orthodox Gauḍīyas reject this (dsp:sahajiya-and-gaudiya-orthodoxy).
summary: The Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā is a Bengali tradition that interiorizes the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa: the divine couple dwell as the innate natures of every woman and man, and through a guru-guided discipline culminating in the ritual union of partners (summary only) human love is refined into divine prema and the sahaja state. Its texts are 17th–18th-century Bengali manuals; its most famous voice is the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās.
notes: Family 'vedic' (as a Vaiṣṇava movement), with the Buddhist Sahajiyā continuity recorded only as a scholarly hypothesis (brw:mahasiddha-to-vaisnava-sahajiya). Sexual-yogic practice: summary and warnings only.

name: Kartābhajā
alt_names: the worshippers of the Kartā (the Master)

tradition.text: Āulcānd appeared as a youth in a betel garden in Nadia and was recognized as Caitanya returned; he departed in the later 18th c.

scholarly.text: late 18th c. origin; Rāmśaraṇ Pāl (d. c. 1783) and Satī Mā organized the community; Rāmdulāl (Dulālcānd, c. 1775–1832) composed the Bhāber Gīt; much growth in 19th-c. Calcutta

transmissions_received.what: Caitanya as the source (Āulcānd as Caitanya returned), Vaiṣṇava vocabulary and kīrtana
sahaja mānuṣa, secrecy, the living human as the site of the divine

distinctive_positions: God is the Kartā, the Master, present as the living guru (Mahāśay); 'worship the human' (mānuṣ bhajan).
Open to all castes and to Muslims; caste distinctions are void within the fellowship.
A double life: 'in the world, worldly custom; with the true guru, oneness' — outward conformity, inner Kartābhajā practice.
The Bhāber Gīt (Songs of Bhāva) as scripture, rich in the mercantile imagery of Calcutta (bazaar, company, trade).
The Dol Pūrṇimā festival at Ghoshpara, with healing at the Himsāgar tank and the pomegranate tree of Satī Mā.
Hereditary Kartā of the Pāl family; disciples (barātī) pay dues through the Mahāśays.
summary: The Kartābhajā is a Bengali sect founded in the late 18th c. around Āulcānd, held to be Caitanya returned, and organized by Rāmśaraṇ Pāl and his wife Satī Mā at Ghoshpara; it worships the Kartā (Master) in the living guru, admits all castes and Muslims, keeps its teaching secret behind outward conformity, and sings the Bhāber Gīt.
notes: Much of its organized history is post-1800 (flagged recent). Scholarly study: H. B. Urban (used only for dating labels).

name: Balarāmī sampradāya

scholarly.text: early 19th c.; Balarām Hāḍi c. 1785–1850

distinctive_positions: Founded by a man of the Hāḍi (sweeper) caste, held by his followers to be the supreme God (Hāḍirām).
Rejection of brahmanical ritual, caste and the Vedic gods; worship of the human.
summary: A small Bengali sect founded by Balarām Hāḍi of Meherpur, of 'untouchable' birth, which rejected caste and brahmanical religion and venerated its founder as God.
notes: Known mainly from 20th-c. ethnographic reports (Sudhir Chakrabarti and others); low confidence.

name: Sāhebdhanī sampradāya

scholarly.text: 18th–19th c.

distinctive_positions: Worship of Dīnadayāl ('merciful to the poor') as the supreme; a mixed Hindu–Muslim membership of low castes.
Songs (notably Kubir Gõsāi's) in the Bāul-Sahajiyā idiom.
summary: A small Bengali sect of low-caste Hindus and Muslims in Nadia, known for its songs (Kubir Gõsāi) in the Sahajiyā-Bāul idiom.
notes: Known mainly from 20th-c. ethnographic reports; low confidence on founder and dates.
